did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 14 opens with the elders of Israel coming to Ezekiel and sitting before him to hear the word of the Lord.
Did you know? The Lord describes the idols as having entered the elders’ hearts, and their sin as a “stumbling block of iniquity” placed before their faces.
Did you know? The prophet calls the people not only to remove their idols, but also to turn their faces toward the Lord—that is, to change direction and return to Him.
Did you know? The warning in this chapter also applies to the foreigner living in Israel: anyone who turns away from the Lord and clings to idols will be held accountable.

Did you know? Ezekiel emphasizes that responsibility rests both on the person who consults the prophet while clinging to sin and on the prophet who is tempted to speak falsely; both will bear their guilt.
Did you know? The purpose of the judgment is that the Israelites will no longer continue to stray from the Lord, but will be His people and He will be their God.
Did you know? Noah, Daniel, and Job are mentioned together as examples of righteousness; yet even they could save by their righteousness only themselves, not the land or their children.

Did you know? The chapter makes clear again that the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job would not extend the benefit of deliverance to their descendants: each would be saved by his own righteousness.
Did you know? Jerusalem is told that the four severe judgments—sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague—will all be sent against it to cut off both people and animals.

Did you know? Despite the destruction, a remnant of sons and daughters will remain in Jerusalem; when the exiles see their ways and actions, they will understand that the destruction did not come without cause.
